cards.scenario: Mobile app, 4 KB prefs per user, millions of users: HA, cheap, scalable, secure?
cards.ok: DynamoDB item per user; web identity federation + STS with fine-grained access; app queries table directly.
cards.bad: Prefs in S3; DynamoDB item points to S3 object; app fetches S3 URL then object.
cards.why: DynamoDB fine-grained access (keys per user) lets the app query directly; the S3-pointer design adds a second hop.

cards.scenario: Delegated account must run AWS RAM org-wide resource sharing; simplest fix?
cards.ok: Enable trusted access with enable-sharing-with-aws-organization in RAM CLI; mirror previous account's config.
cards.bad: Enable cross-account access with AWS Organizations in the RAM console; mirror config.
cards.why: RAM needs trusted access enabled with Organizations; a console cross-account toggle is not the mechanism.

cards.scenario: Notify on any change to AWS Organizations accounts after suspected breach (select two).
cards.ok: CloudTrail trail for Organizations API calls + AWS Config monitoring, alerts via EventBridge/SNS.
cards.bad: CloudWatch Dashboard monitoring Organizations changes, with an SNS topic notification.
cards.why: Dashboards watch resource metrics, not Organizations changes; use CloudTrail API logging plus Config.

cards.scenario: Restrict which AWS services each member account may use, LEAST complexity?
cards.ok: AWS Organizations with Service Control Policies controlling allowed services per member account.
cards.bad: Organizations OUs plus a custom IAM policy per account to allow or deny services.
cards.why: SCPs centrally cap services per account; per-account custom IAM policies add needless complexity.

cards.scenario: New account needs Config rule changes despite root SCP; no long-term overhead.
cards.ok: Move SCPs from root to Production OU; temporary Onboarding OU permits Config changes.
cards.bad: Keep root SCP; park new account in temporary Onboarding OU whose SCP allows Config.
cards.why: Explicit deny inherited from the root cannot be overridden by an allow in a child OU.

cards.scenario: Cross-account copy of shared resources plus continuous policy audit: which policy type?
cards.ok: Resource-based policy for cross-account access, audited with AWS Config rules.
cards.bad: Cross-account access via user-based (identity) policy, audited with AWS Config rules.
cards.why: Resource-based policy fits sharing across accounts; Config (not Systems Manager) audits policy compliance.

cards.scenario: Mobile app for LDAP employees: authentication plus AWS authorization (select two).
cards.ok: Custom SAML solution over LDAP using IAM IdP assertion; custom OIDC auth + Cognito Identity Pools.
cards.bad: Custom SAML authentication, with AWS IAM Identity Center authorizing AWS resource access.
cards.why: IAM Identity Center supports browser-based SSO only, not mobile apps; use IAM IdP or Cognito identity pools.

cards.scenario: Consolidated billing: keep one business unit's Reserved Instance discounts unshared.
cards.ok: Turn off RI sharing on the management account for that unit's member accounts.
cards.bad: Set RI sharing to private on the business unit's own account.
cards.why: RI sharing is switched off from the management account; no per-account private setting exists.

cards.scenario: ReactJS photo and caption app on DynamoDB/S3: most cost-effective scalable access?
cards.ok: Web identity provider login; STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity issues temporary credentials via an IAM role.
cards.bad: Temporary credentials from a Token Vending Machine running on a single EC2 instance.
cards.why: Single-EC2 TVM is a single point of failure; web identity federation avoids it.

cards.scenario: SCP applied to new account, yet ECS-related actions still allowed. Likely reason?
cards.ok: SCPs do not affect service-linked roles.
cards.bad: An SCP on a higher-level OU permits the actions and overrides the administrator's SCP.
cards.why: Service-linked roles are exempt from SCPs, so the restriction cannot apply to them.

cards.scenario: Fashion mobile app, millions of users: user data, photos, 100-character captions.
cards.ok: Cognito for auth, DynamoDB for user data, S3 for photos, CloudFront for static content.
cards.bad: Cognito for auth with an RDS database for user data; S3 photos; CloudFront.
cards.why: Same stack but RDS; DynamoDB is the scalable store for small mobile user records.

cards.scenario: Single 1 Gbps Direct Connect to 10 VPCs: most cost-effective redundancy?
cards.ok: VPN tunnels from on-premises to each VPC's virtual private gateway, BGP for routing.
cards.bad: Second 1 Gbps Direct Connect with private VIFs to all 10 VPCs, BGP peering.
cards.why: VPN is the cost-effective backup; another Direct Connect connection is not.

cards.scenario: Link multi-Region VPCs to on-premises office: private, predictable performance, low overhead.
cards.ok: Direct Connect gateway: virtual private gateway per VPC, private VIF per Direct Connect connection.
cards.bad: Hub-and-spoke with Transit Gateway, VPCs and on-premises routed over Site-to-Site VPN.
cards.why: Dedicated private network with predictable performance needs Direct Connect; Transit Gateway over VPN lacks it.

cards.scenario: Central VPC to team VPCs, no public Internet; alert on denied requests with source IP.
cards.ok: VPC peering to each team VPC; Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs capture rejected traffic and source IPs.
cards.bad: IPSec tunnels between central and team VPCs; Flow Logs capture rejected traffic.
cards.why: IPSec tunnels traverse the public Internet; VPC peering stays on the AWS network.

cards.scenario: Intermittent outbound API failures in one AZ via EC2 NAT instances; cause and fix?
cards.ok: A failed NAT instance in a public subnet; replace with NAT Gateways for availability and scalability.
cards.bad: Overloaded NAT instance; scale NAT instances to larger sizes.
cards.why: NAT instance failure is the weak point; managed NAT Gateways give availability and scalability.

cards.scenario: 50 accounts share private DNS names across VPCs: LEAST complex DNS architecture.
cards.ok: RAM-shared services VPC peered to each VPC; one private hosted zone; programmatically associate other VPCs.
cards.bad: Per-account private hosted zones with Name Server entries pointing at the central account DNS.
cards.why: Private zone must be associated with each VPC; NS delegation to central account does not resolve.

cards.scenario: Fargate task in private subnet cannot pull image from ECR; fix?
cards.ok: Disable auto-assign public IP; NAT gateway in a public subnet; route private subnet through it.
cards.bad: Same setup, but launch the NAT gateway in the private subnet.
cards.why: A NAT gateway needs a public IP and an IGW route, so it belongs in a public subnet.

cards.scenario: Employees reach VPC over existing Direct Connect with encryption; keep DX performance.
cards.ok: Public VIF; Site-to-Site VPN with BGP running over the Direct Connect connection.
cards.bad: Private VIF; Site-to-Site VPN with BGP over the Direct Connect connection.
cards.why: Encrypted VPN over Direct Connect requires a public VIF, not a private one.

cards.scenario: Read-heavy app, North America and Asia users: fault tolerant, multi-Region, DB semantics preserved (select two).
cards.ok: Route 53 geolocation plus failover health checks; active-active ASGs with Aurora global database.
cards.bad: Route 53 geoproximity plus multivalue answer routing with health checks.
cards.why: Multivalue can misroute users; two writable MySQL masters can't sync, Aurora global database can.

cards.scenario: Central DB reachable by name from peered VPCs, internal use only: Route 53 setup?
cards.ok: Private hosted zone associated with the VPCs; A record to the database server IP.
cards.bad: Public hosted zone associated with the VPCs; A record to the IP.
cards.why: Internal-only access needs a private hosted zone, not a public one.

cards.scenario: Global serverless forex app slow for users: improve performance, minimal cost (select two).
cards.ok: CloudFront origin group failover plus Lambda@Edge running authentication closer to users.
cards.bad: Deploy the application to multiple Regions with Route 53 latency routing.
cards.why: Multi-Region deployment is costly; CloudFront origin failover plus Lambda@Edge is the minimal-cost fix.

cards.scenario: Fargate e-commerce behind CloudFront: MOST secure against DNS spoofing and SSL hijacking.
cards.ok: Route 53 registration with DNSSEC on public hosted zones; ACM-issued 2048-bit certificate.
cards.bad: Third-party DNS with customer-managed DNSSEC keys; ACM-generated 2048-bit certificate.
cards.why: Route 53 supports DNSSEC signing natively; a third-party DNS provider is unnecessary.

cards.scenario: Account B VPC cannot resolve Account A private hosted zone records (select two).
cards.ok: Account A authorizes the VPC association; Account B associates its VPC, then deletes the authorization.
cards.bad: Peer the two VPCs and use Account A's DNS resolver IPs from Account B.
cards.why: Cross-account private zones need authorization plus association; VPC peering alone doesn't resolve them.

cards.scenario: CloudFront payments: encrypt card data and improve cache hit ratio.
cards.ok: HTTPS to origin plus field-level encryption; long Cache-Control max-age on objects.
cards.bad: Signed URLs plus a long Cache-Control max-age on objects.
cards.why: Signed URLs restrict private content but do not encrypt card fields; field-level encryption does.

cards.scenario: Multi-Region app on ALBs for US and Europe users: best global entry with Route 53?
cards.ok: Global Accelerator with endpoint groups on regional ALBs; Route 53 public alias record to the accelerator.
cards.bad: Global Accelerator plus a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint pointing the domain at the accelerator.
cards.why: Resolver inbound endpoints serve DNS queries into VPCs; use a public alias record for the accelerator.

cards.scenario: Expanding web apps to new Regions: keep HTTPS working for each FQDN.
cards.ok: Request certificates in AWS Certificate Manager in each new Region; attach to the local ALB.
cards.bad: Request ACM certificates once in US West and reuse them on ALBs in all Regions.
cards.why: ACM certificates are Regional, so request one per Region; KMS does not issue TLS certificates.

cards.scenario: Dynamic travel site on-premises overwhelmed by traffic: stay functional, block SQL injection and XSS.
cards.ok: CloudFront caches images and static assets; AWS WAF on the distribution blocks web attacks.
cards.bad: Move site to S3 static hosting, point Route 53 domain at it, KMS-encrypt.
cards.why: Site is dynamic (payments, bookings), so S3 static hosting fails; CloudFront plus WAF fits.

cards.scenario: Block blacklisted countries yet serve globally at low latency, to avoid penalties.
cards.ok: CloudFront distribution with geo restriction blocking the blacklisted countries.
cards.bad: Route 53 geolocation routing policy that blocks traffic from the blacklisted countries.
cards.why: Route 53 only resolves DNS; it can't block traffic or cut latency. CloudFront geo restriction does.

cards.scenario: S3 static website www.tutorialsdojo.com with Route 53 records not working; most likely cause?
cards.ok: The bucket lacks public read access, blocking visitors.
cards.bad: Route 53 is still propagating changes; wait 12 hours.
cards.why: Route 53 propagates quickly; missing public read on the bucket is the real blocker.

cards.scenario: Fargate WordPress: pass DB credentials as environment variables securely, least effort.
cards.ok: Secrets Manager with KMS; ECS task execution role referenced in the task definition.
cards.bad: Parameter Store encrypted with KMS; ECS task execution role referenced in the task definition.
cards.why: Parameter Store lacks dedicated secret storage with lifecycle management and key rotation; Secrets Manager has them.

cards.scenario: Dev containers on-premises, prod on Fargate: MOST operationally efficient, consistent tooling.
cards.ok: Amazon ECS Anywhere: one standard container orchestrator for on-premises and AWS.
cards.bad: Amazon EKS Anywhere to manage on-premises Kubernetes.
cards.why: EKS Anywhere isn't designed to run in AWS; ECS Anywhere spans on-premises and Fargate.

cards.scenario: Monthly HPC image processing, 10 PB: cost-effective, less management, same durability.
cards.ok: AWS Batch with managed compute environment on Spot Instances; raw data in S3.
cards.bad: SQS job queue, Spot Auto Scaling group, raw data shared through EFS.
cards.why: Batch is managed; EFS costs more than S3 and listing jobs on SQS may process some twice.

cards.scenario: Three-tier product site must handle 300,000 peak users: cost-effective AWS design.
cards.ok: CloudFormation stack: Multi-AZ Auto Scaling EC2 behind an ALB, with Aurora MySQL.
cards.bad: ECS cluster on Spot Instances across AZs behind an ALB, with RDS MySQL.
cards.why: Spot capacity can be reclaimed, hurting site reliability; Multi-AZ ASG with Aurora is dependable.

cards.scenario: 16 TiB MySQL on EC2 plus Rails app: MOST cost-effective, highly available 24x7.
cards.ok: Smaller EC2 in Auto Scaling behind ALB with Reserved base; migrate to Aurora with cross-AZ replica.
cards.bad: Same app tier, but RDS MySQL Multi-AZ with storage adjusted manually.
cards.why: Aurora scales storage automatically by default; manual RDS storage adjustment is unnecessary effort.

cards.scenario: Replace ALB/EC2 app with serverless; build, test and deploy gradually.
cards.ok: AWS SAM with CodeBuild, CodeDeploy and CodePipeline CI/CD pipeline.
cards.bad: CodePipeline CI/CD plus Systems Manager Automation for builds and gradual deployments.
cards.why: Systems Manager Automation manages instances, not serverless builds and deployments; SAM fits serverless.

cards.scenario: Deploy Node.js app to EC2 and on-premises with RDS credentials, MOST secure automation.
cards.ok: SecureString in Parameter Store; EC2 gets IAM role, on-premises servers a service role; CodeDeploy.
cards.bad: Secrets Manager credentials with rotation; deploy to on-premises servers via Elastic Beanstalk.
cards.why: Elastic Beanstalk can't deploy to on-premises servers; CodeDeploy can.

cards.scenario: Docker apps on self-managed VMs: migrate for agility, use OpenJDK, minimal app change.
cards.ok: Re-platform: Docker on ECS, images in ECR, MySQL migrated to RDS with DMS.
cards.bad: Re-host: mirror current servers on EC2 and run Docker there.
cards.why: Re-hosting ignores cloud elasticity and agility; re-platform gains them without major app changes.

cards.scenario: EKS on EC2 with RDS: minimize compute cost during peak surges.
cards.ok: Compute Savings Plans baseline, Spot for peaks, 1-year All Upfront RI for database.
cards.bad: Compute Savings Plans baseline, On-Demand Capacity Reservations for peaks, 1-year No Upfront RI.
cards.why: Capacity Reservations ensure capacity, not savings; Spot is the cheapest answer for peak surges.

cards.scenario: ECS CRM microservices: container-level network monitoring, security groups; MOST secure.
cards.ok: awsvpc network mode, security groups on tasks, IAM roles for tasks.
cards.bad: awsvpc mode, security groups on tasks, but pass IAM credentials into the container at launch.
cards.why: Passing credentials into containers is insecure; IAM roles for tasks supply temporary credentials.

cards.scenario: Migrate NGINX plus MySQL car registration site to AWS behind a load balancer; most efficient?
cards.ok: Two NGINX EC2 instances in two AZs, DMS for database, ELB, Route 53 alias A record.
cards.bad: DataSync web files to S3, run site from S3, DMS plus SCT, Route 53 alias.
cards.why: A dynamic site cannot be hosted from S3; EC2 behind an ELB can.

cards.scenario: Stateless web tier peak load: cost-effective quick recovery if an AZ fails.
cards.ok: Spot Fleet with diversified allocation and Auto Scaling per AZ for peak; keep steady-state setup.
cards.bad: Auto Scaling groups of Reserved Instances per AZ to handle peak load.
cards.why: Reserved Instances cost more than Spot for peaks; diversified Spot Fleet adds AZ resilience.

cards.scenario: Internal Dockerized app with MySQL, 5+ years, lowest possible cost.
cards.ok: ECS on Spot with draining; Reserved RDS plus replicas; encrypted S3 with Glacier lifecycle for documents.
cards.bad: ECS on Spot with Aurora Serverless v2; documents on a shared encrypted EBS volume.
cards.why: Documents belong in S3 with lifecycle rules; EBS storage is costly and Aurora Serverless v2 may cost more.

cards.scenario: CloudFormation stack deletion must keep RDS and S3 data: right DeletionPolicy?
cards.ok: DeletionPolicy Snapshot on RDS; Retain on the S3 bucket.
cards.bad: DeletionPolicy Retain on both the RDS instance and the S3 bucket.
cards.why: RDS should use Snapshot so its backup is kept; S3 uses Retain (snapshot isn't valid for it).

cards.scenario: IoT pet collar biometrics: real-time analytics dashboard and storage architecture.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Streams ingest, Kinesis analysis to real-time dashboard, aggregate to S3, store in Redshift.
cards.bad: SQS queue collects data, Kinesis analyzes it, results stored in RDS MySQL.
cards.why: Real-time analytics needs Kinesis Data Streams ingestion, not SQS or EMR collection.

cards.scenario: FIFA World Cup stats: tens of millions of report queries, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: RDS Multi-AZ with replicas; batch job writes reports to S3; CloudFront caches with daily TTL.
cards.bad: Multi-AZ RDS, reports generated via ElastiCache with default expiry.
cards.why: S3 gives durable report storage and CloudFront the CDN; ElastiCache or replicas alone lack both.

cards.scenario: ASG web app failed on database overload and health checks; prevent recurrence (select two).
cards.ok: ElastiCache caching frequent DB queries; ALB health check on simple HTML page, not DB page.
cards.bad: Switch ALB target group health check to TCP checks on the EC2 instances.
cards.why: ALB supports only HTTP/HTTPS health checks, not TCP.

cards.scenario: Videos land in DLQ without errors; visibility timeout 1h, maxReceiveCount 1. Fix?
cards.ok: Raise redrive policy maxReceiveCount to 10 so consumers retry before the dead-letter queue.
cards.bad: Raise the queue visibility timeout to 2 hours.
cards.why: Longer visibility timeout only helps if processing outlasts it; videos didn't, retries were the problem.

cards.scenario: Single EC2 plus EBS immigration system: highly available, scalable storage and task distribution.
cards.ok: S3 with cross-region replication for files; SQS queue with Auto Scaling EC2 workers.
cards.bad: Provisioned IOPS EBS storage with SQS queue and Auto Scaling workers.
cards.why: EBS isn't easily scalable or durable like S3; per-instance EBS volumes are uneconomical and hard to sync.

cards.scenario: IoT files land in S3 every 5 minutes; process into RDS fast, least effort.
cards.ok: Lambda replaces the cron job, triggered by S3 object-created event notifications.
cards.bad: Lambda triggered by an EventBridge rule on CloudTrail S3 data events.
cards.why: S3 event notifications trigger Lambda directly; CloudTrail plus EventBridge adds unneeded setup.

cards.scenario: Cloud call center: inbound calls, speech chatbot, query business apps for callers.
cards.ok: Amazon Connect contact center integrated with an Amazon Lex chatbot for speech and intent.
cards.bad: Amazon Connect integrated with an Amazon Comprehend chatbot.
cards.why: Lex provides speech recognition and intent understanding; Comprehend only analyzes text.

cards.scenario: Smartwatch stats, 10-15 TB per year, 120-day retention: most cost-effective storage.
cards.ok: DynamoDB table with scaling and TTL deleting records after 120 days.
cards.bad: Aurora Serverless with a nightly Lambda deleting records older than 120 days.
cards.why: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired records natively; Aurora needs custom scheduled cleanup.

cards.scenario: Global mobile marketplace: multi-Region transactions, scalable, cost-effective, highly available.
cards.ok: DynamoDB global table; each Region writes locally and changes replicate automatically.
cards.bad: Per-Region DynamoDB tables with Lambda replaying recent writes to other Regions.
cards.why: Custom Lambda replication doesn't scale to millions of users; global tables replicate natively.

cards.scenario: Lambda waits on on-premises MySQL over VPN, costs soaring: reduce overall cost.
cards.ok: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ; API Gateway caching cuts Lambda invocations; lower Lambda timeout and memory.
cards.bad: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ; CloudFront in front of API Gateway caches API responses.
cards.why: API caching belongs on API Gateway, not CloudFront.

cards.scenario: Heterogeneous on-premises database migration to RDS PostgreSQL needing schema and code conversion.
cards.ok: AWS SCT converts the schema; AWS DMS migrates data to RDS for PostgreSQL.
cards.bad: Application Migration Service first, then DMS converts and migrates to PostgreSQL.
cards.why: SCT converts schema and code before DMS moves data; Application Migration Service rehosts servers.

cards.scenario: Migrate three-tier VMs: continuous sync, test before cutover, minimal operational overhead.
cards.ok: Transform MGN with replication agent per server; continuous replication; test instances, then cutover.
cards.bad: Transform MGN for root volumes only; import data volumes with import-snapshot.
cards.why: Splitting root and data volumes adds complexity and inconsistency risk; MGN replicates all volumes.

cards.scenario: Media archive plus Rekognition face search: LEAST ongoing overhead, MINIMAL disruption.
cards.ok: File gateway on-premises; MAM writes media files to it; Rekognition builds a face collection.
cards.bad: Tape gateway storing to Glacier, with a Rekognition face collection.
cards.why: Tape gateway data can't be fetched in real time; file gateway keeps the MAM workflow intact.

cards.scenario: Online delivery DR: meet RTO/RPO cost-effectively, protect sensitive data.
cards.ok: Hourly DB backups to S3, transaction logs to S3 every 5 minutes, Macie for sensitive data.
cards.bad: 15-minute DB backups to Glacier, 5-minute transaction logs to S3, with Macie.
cards.why: Glacier retrievals take hours, missing the RTO; Macie, not Shield, finds sensitive data.

cards.scenario: Newspaper page search site moving to AWS: scalable, durable, highly available.
cards.ok: Scanned images in S3 served via CloudFront; multi-AZ Beanstalk web tier; OpenSearch Service for search.
cards.bad: EBS-backed EC2 with ALB and NGINX; images on EBS with Data Lifecycle Manager.
cards.why: S3 with CloudFront and OpenSearch is more durable and scalable than EC2/EBS-hosted images.

cards.scenario: Partner company's heavy S3 downloads raise the startup's transfer costs; lower them.
cards.ok: Enable Requester Pays on the S3 buckets so the media company pays for transfer.
cards.bad: Provide cross-account bucket access; retrieval is charged to the requesting account.
cards.why: Without Requester Pays the bucket owner pays; enabling it shifts transfer cost to the requester.

cards.scenario: Global tracking app DR with StackSets in two Regions, automatic failback; NoSQL database.
cards.ok: Route 53 failover routing plus a DynamoDB global table spanning both Regions.
cards.bad: Route 53 failover routing plus an Aurora global database spanning both Regions.
cards.why: App is designed for NoSQL, so DynamoDB global tables fit; Aurora is not recommended.

cards.scenario: Move 60 TB SQL Server warehouse to Redshift in 30 days over 50 Mbps, cheapest.
cards.ok: Data Transfer Terminal slot; SCT prepares schema and data; upload bulk historical data at the facility.
cards.bad: Terminal upload, then import through RDS for Oracle and SCT/DMS to Redshift.
cards.why: No RDS Oracle detour is needed; SCT prepares the data directly for Redshift.

cards.scenario: Serverless portal hit by SQL injection: most suitable, cost-effective protection.
cards.ok: AWS WAF web ACL in front of API Gateway blocking SQL injection; AWS Config tracks ACL changes.
cards.bad: AWS WAF web ACL in front of the Lambda functions; Firewall Manager tracks ACL changes.
cards.why: WAF attaches in front of API Gateway, not Lambda; Firewall Manager is for multi-account management.

cards.scenario: Block port-scanning IP immediately and defend against network and transport-layer DDoS.
cards.ok: Deny the IP in the Network ACL; protect with AWS Shield Advanced.
cards.bad: Deny the IP via Security Group rules; use AWS WAF and AWS Config.
cards.why: Security groups can't deny; block the IP at the Network ACL. Shield Advanced covers DDoS.

cards.scenario: Windows EC2 fleet: enforce approved patches and AMIs, alert on non-compliance (select two).
cards.ok: Systems Manager Patch Manager patch baseline + AWS Config approved-AMIs managed rule with CloudWatch alarms.
cards.bad: GuardDuty monitoring patches and unapproved AMIs, with CloudWatch alarms for non-compliant instances.
cards.why: GuardDuty detects threats, not patch or AMI compliance; use Patch Manager and AWS Config.

cards.scenario: CloudTrail audit of account activity across Regions; protect log confidentiality.
cards.ok: Global-services trail, one new S3 bucket, IAM roles, bucket policies, and MFA Delete.
cards.bad: Trail with global services using an existing S3 bucket, S3 ACLs and MFA Delete.
cards.why: An existing bucket may already be accessible; use a new bucket secured by IAM roles and policies.

cards.scenario: Mitigate DDoS for AWS-hosted web applications (select two).
cards.ok: CloudFront for static and dynamic content with alarms/Auto Scaling; ALB plus AWS WAF.
cards.bad: Reserved EC2 instances for maximum performance plus AWS WAF.
cards.why: Reserved instances add no extra performance; absorb attacks with CloudFront, ALB and WAF.

cards.scenario: Bank web app with sensitive data: protect SSL private key, durable encrypted logs, highly available.
cards.ok: TCP load balancing; CloudHSM across two AZs performs SSL; logs to private SSE S3 bucket.
cards.bad: TCP load balancing; a single CloudHSM performs SSL; logs to private encrypted S3.
cards.why: A single CloudHSM is a single point of failure; two AZs give high availability.

cards.scenario: CloudTrail audit of all account activity across Regions; encrypt and protect logs.
cards.ok: CloudTrail trail with multi-region and global service events, KMS encryption, MFA Delete on S3.
cards.bad: CloudTrail trail with multi-region but no-include-global-service-events.
cards.why: Complete audit needs both multi-region and global-service flags; a 'CloudWatch trail' does not exist.

cards.scenario: Aggregate on-premises app logs, detect errors, notify Ops at threshold: MOST suitable.
cards.ok: CloudWatch agent to CloudWatch Logs, metric filter, CloudWatch Alarm notifies Ops.
cards.bad: CloudWatch agent sends logs to EventBridge; Athena monitors the metric filter.
cards.why: Logs go to CloudWatch Logs, not EventBridge; alarm on the metric filter.

cards.scenario: ASG instances terminate as unhealthy, logs inconclusive: quickest way to troubleshoot?
cards.ok: Suspend the ASG Terminate process; open Session Manager on an unhealthy instance.
cards.bad: Enable termination protection on a new instance, then use Session Manager.
cards.why: Termination protection doesn't stop the ASG; suspend its Terminate process instead.

cards.scenario: Fargate task count nearing quota: alert at 75 percent, MOST operationally efficient.
cards.ok: Alarm on AWS/Usage quota metric via SERVICE_QUOTA math expression above 75 percent; notify via SNS.
cards.bad: Alarm on ECS sample count metric divided by SERVICE_QUOTA above 75 percent.
cards.why: Sample count measures requests, not quota usage; AWS/Usage metrics track quota consumption.

cards.scenario: App needs 500 GB static data, daily deploys, OS patches within 48 hours: cost-effective?
cards.ok: Systems Manager patches and bakes new AMI; CodeDeploy deploys app; shared EFS volume.
cards.bad: Amazon Linux AMI; user data downloads 500 GB from S3; Systems Manager patches instances.
cards.why: Every instance downloading 500 GB to EBS is wasteful; use baked AMIs, CodeDeploy and shared EFS.

cards.scenario: Patch hundreds of Windows EC2 on schedule without all going down together.
cards.ok: Two patch groups, default baseline, two non-overlapping maintenance windows running AWS-RunPatchBaseline.
cards.bad: One patch group on a single maintenance window.
cards.why: One group patches everything at once; two groups on non-overlapping windows avoid unavailability.

cards.scenario: Patch prod, dev, test with different baselines, LEAST effort using Systems Manager.
cards.ok: Tag instances by environment and OS; baseline per environment; Patch Groups apply them.
cards.bad: Tag instances by OS only; baseline per environment; Patch Groups apply them.
cards.why: Patch Groups need environment tags to map each environment to its own baseline.

cards.scenario: Collect and analyze Windows and Linux EC2 logs with minimal effort.
cards.ok: Unified CloudWatch agent pushes logs to CloudWatch Logs; analyze with Logs Insights.
cards.bad: SSM Agent collects and pushes logs to CloudWatch Logs; analyze with Logs Insights.
cards.why: The CloudWatch agent collects logs; SSM Agent manages instances, not log shipping.
